$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{(y-2)^{2}}{4}-\frac{(x+2)^{2}}{9} & =1 \\ \frac{(0-2)^{2}}{4}-\frac{(x+2)^{2}}{9} & =1 \\ 1-\frac{(x+2)^{2}}{9} & =1 \\ \frac{(x+2)^{2}}{9} & =0 \\ (x+2)^{2} & =0 \\ x+2 & =0 \\ x & =-2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the $x$-intercept is $(-2,0).$

\begin{aligned}\frac{{y}^{2}}{3}-\frac{{x}^{2}}{12} & =1 \\ \frac{{x}^{2}}{3}-\frac{{x}^{2}}{12} & =1 \\ \frac{12{x}^{2}}{36}-\frac{3{x}^{2}}{36} & =1 \\ \frac{9{x}^{2}}{36} & =1 \\ {x}^{2} & =4 \\ x & =\pm 2\end{aligned}
$$

So, in ascending order, the $x$-coordinates of the points of intersection are
$x=-2$ and $x=2.$

To find the $x$-intercepts of the hyperbola, we substitute $y=0$ into the equation of the hyperbola and solve for $x,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{(x+1)^{2}}{10}-\frac{{y}^{2}}{25} & =1 \\ \frac{(x+1)^{2}}{10}-\frac{{0}^{2}}{25} & =1 \\ \frac{(x+1)^{2}}{10} & =1 \\ (x+1)^{2} & =10 \\ x+1 & =\pm \sqrt{10} \\ x & =-1\pm \sqrt{10}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the $x$-intercepts are $\left(-1\pm \sqrt{10},0\right).$

canonical_examples.problem:
Calculate the points where the hyperbola 
$\dfrac{x^2}{10}-\dfrac{y^2}{15}=1$
intersects the line $y=-3.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
To find the points where the hyperbola intersects the line $y=-3,$ we substitute $y=-3$ into the equation of the hyperbola and solve for $x,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{x}^{2}}{10}-\frac{{y}^{2}}{15} & =1 \\ \frac{{x}^{2}}{10}-\frac{(-3)^{2}}{15} & =1 \\ \frac{{x}^{2}}{10}-\frac{9}{15} & =1 \\ \frac{{x}^{2}}{10}-\frac{3}{5} & =1 \\ {x}^{2}-6 & =10 \\ {x}^{2} & =16 \\ x & =\pm 4\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the hyperbola intersects the horizontal line $y=-3$ at the points $(\pm 4, -3).$

tutorials.name: Finding Intersections of Hyperbolas and Lines
tutorials.problem:
Let's now consider the hyperbola $\dfrac {x^2}{9} - \dfrac {y ^2}{3} = 1$ and the line $x = 6.$ The hyperbola and the line intersect at the points $A$ and $B,$ as shown in the diagram below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14192928/assets/fade29777e50e807aabb1f26f129669ae8b999235efb6c9bf72f11dcbfbb0a2e.png)

To find the points where the hyperbola intersects the line, we substitute the equation of the line, $x=6,$ into the equation of the hyperbola and solve for $y,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{x}^{2}}{9}-\frac{{y}^{2}}{3} & =1 \\ \frac{{6}^{2}}{9}-\frac{{y}^{2}}{3} & =1 \\ \frac{36}{9}-\frac{{y}^{2}}{3} & =1 \\ 4-\frac{{y}^{2}}{3} & =1 \\ \frac{{y}^{2}}{3} & =4-1 \\ \frac{{y}^{2}}{3} & =3 \\ {y}^{2} & =9 \\ y & =\pm 3\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the hyperbola intersects the line $x=6$ at the points $\left(6, \pm3\right).$
